bib.title: Bandit Algorithms, Chapter 32: Ranking
bib.venue: book chapter (Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press)

question: How can a learner choose rankings of m items out of l over n rounds from click feedback with regret that does not scale with the number of rankings?
hypothesis: Assuming a click model in which click probability depends on item attractiveness and position makes ranking learnable; the generic model generalises document-based, position-based and cascade models.
contributions: Click models: document-based, position-based, cascade, generic (Assumption 32.1)
TopRank policy (Lattimore et al. 2018) with gap-dependent and worst-case regret bounds
Notes on CascadeUCB/KL-UCB, linear features, adversarial ranked bandits

limits: Authors: 'there is still a long way to go before we have a genuinely practical algorithm for large-scale online ranking problems.'
Regret is linear in l, unpleasant for many items; linear-feature variants only mentioned (Zong 2016, Li 2019a), not analysed.
Assumption 32.1(c) fourth-position part is 'perhaps the most easily criticised assumption' (less attractive early items raise later examination).
No experiments or numeric examples in the chapter; no pseudocode listing for CascadeUCB, only prose in Note 2.
Probabilistic ranking principle (independence between documents) criticised for ignoring diversity (Exercise 32.2); not modelled here.
Regret bound uses delta=1/n; algorithm needs n only to set delta; c ~ 3.43 from Exercise 20.10 (not in this chapter).
practices: Choose the click model by how the list is shown and whether a click leaves the page: cascade when clicking diverts to another page, position-based otherwise (p.389-390).
Randomise item order within each block so that position effects average out and click differences identify attractiveness order (TopRank step 2, p.392).
Only compare two items when they share a block; accumulate S_tij = sum of (C_ti - C_tj) and add (j,i) to G when S_tij >= sqrt(2 N_tij log(c sqrt(N_tij)/delta)) (step 3, p.393).
Under independent-Bernoulli cascade, use optimistic ranking: sort items by UCB on alpha and shortlist top m (CascadeUCB); prefer KL-UCB since most items have barely positive attractiveness (p.399).
When l is large, put linear structure alpha(i)=<theta, phi_i> on items (p.399).
When ranking is adversarial and offline optimum is NP-hard, use a greedy approximation (p.399-400).

figures.caption: A classic ranking problem: which hats to put where on the stand? Higher and towards the front attracts more attention.

Part (c) of Assumption 32.1 says that the probability of clicking in the second position on the left list is larger than the probability of clicking on the second position on the right list by a factor of alpha(i)/alpha(j). For the fourth position, the probability is larger for the right list than the left by the same factor.
figures.why: Shows swapping items i and j and the alpha ratio in the generic assumption.
